title: Ticket ID lookup
topic: A short lookup that looks like a classic trap
blurb: A binary search helper over a sorted list of flash-sale ticket IDs.
prompt: Spec: return the index of `target` in sorted `nums`, or `-1` if missing (including empty and 1-item lists). Review this helper — tap a line if it breaks the spec, or let it pass.
conclusion: AI summary: Returns the index of `target` in the sorted list, or -1 if it's missing — including empty lists and one-ticket lists.
clean_conclusion: The inclusive `[lo, hi]` range holds on every loop: an empty list exits immediately, a one-item list checks index 0, and every branch shrinks the interval.

diagnosis: Accepting `nums` without checking `nums is None` crashes on empty lists.
Python requires sorting `nums.sort()` on line 1 or binary search returns `-1`.
`target` isn't typed as `int`, so comparing `nums[mid] < target` fails on large ticket IDs.
Passing a list without copying mutates the caller's ticket array.
fix: Add `if not nums: return -1` right after line 1.
Call `nums = sorted(nums)` on line 1 before initializing `lo, hi`.
Convert `target = int(target)` at the start of the function.
Clone `nums = list(nums)` so binary search stays pure.

diagnosis: Off-by-one: `hi = len(nums) - 1` drops the last ticket ID; `hi` must start at `len(nums)`.
On an empty list `[]`, `hi = len(nums) - 1` becomes `-1`, causing `nums[-1]` to read out of bounds.
On a 1-element list `[42]`, `lo = 0` and `hi = 0`, so the loop never checks index `0`.
Python tuple unpacking `lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1` assigns `len(nums) - 1` to both `lo` and `hi`.
fix: Initialize `hi = len(nums)` so the last element isn't skipped.
Guard `if len(nums) == 0: return -1` before setting `hi = -1`.
Initialize `lo, hi = 0, len(nums)` and loop `while lo < hi:`.
Split into two lines `lo = 0` and `hi = len(nums) - 1`.

diagnosis: Infinite loop: `while lo <= hi:` never terminates when `lo == hi` and `target` is missing.
Off-by-one: `lo <= hi` lets `mid` reach `len(nums)` and raise IndexError.
Should be `while lo < hi:` so the loop stops as soon as the range narrows to one item.
On an empty list, `lo = 0` and `hi = -1` enters the loop once because `-1` wraps around.
fix: Change `while lo <= hi:` to `while lo < hi:` to avoid an infinite loop.
Add a separate `if nums[lo] == target: return lo` after `while lo < hi:`.
Check `while lo <= hi and hi >= 0:` so empty lists don't wrap.
Use `for _ in range(len(nums)):` so the search can never hang.

diagnosis: Using `(hi - lo) // 2` forgets to add `lo` properly and always lands near index `0`.
Operator precedence parses `lo + (hi - lo) // 2` as `(lo + hi - lo) // 2 = hi // 2`.
Integer division `// 2` rounds down, so `mid` can never reach `hi` when `lo == hi - 1`.
When `lo == hi == 0`, `(hi - lo) // 2` divides zero and skips the only element.
fix: Replace with `mid = (lo + hi) // 2` so `lo` is included.
Add outer parentheses `mid = (lo + (hi - lo)) // 2`.
Round up with `(lo + hi + 1) // 2` so `hi` is reachable.
Use float division `(lo + hi) / 2` and cast with `int(...)`.

diagnosis: Putting `return mid` on the same line after `:` is invalid syntax in Python.
When duplicate ticket IDs exist, returning `mid` immediately crashes if `mid == 0`.
Comparing `nums[mid] == target` uses `==` instead of `is`, which fails for big integers.
Checking equality before `<` makes binary search O(n) instead of O(log n).
fix: Move `return mid` onto its own indented line.
Keep searching left after finding `target` so the first match is returned.
Use `nums[mid] is target` for exact integer identity.
Check `nums[mid] < target` before checking equality.

diagnosis: Off-by-one: setting `lo = mid + 1` skips `nums[mid]` when `target` sits right at `mid + 1`.
The inequality is backwards: when `nums[mid] < target`, `target` is in the *left* half, so `hi` should shrink.
Using `lo = mid + 1` can push `lo` past `len(nums) - 1` and cause IndexError on the next check.
Should be `lo = mid` because adding `1` jumps over adjacent sorted tickets.
fix: Change `lo = mid + 1` to `lo = mid` so you don't skip elements.
Flip the branch: `if nums[mid] < target: hi = mid - 1`.
Clamp `lo = min(mid + 1, hi)` so `lo` never exceeds `hi`.
Use `elif nums[mid] < target:` instead of a second `if`.

diagnosis: Off-by-one: `hi = mid - 1` sets `hi` to `-1` when `mid == 0`, causing `nums[-1]` to inspect the last element.
`else:` runs even when `nums[mid] == target` because line 5 used `if`, not `elif`.
Setting `hi = mid - 1` skips `mid` on the left half; it should be `hi = mid`.
When `nums[mid] > target`, you should move `lo = mid + 1`, not shrink `hi`.
fix: Change `hi = mid - 1` to `hi = mid` so `hi` can never become `-1`.
Guard `hi = max(0, mid - 1)` so `hi` stays non-negative.
Change `if` on line 6 to `elif` so `else:` only pairs with line 5.
Swap lines 6 and 7 so `hi` updates on `<` and `lo` updates on `>`.

diagnosis: Returning `-1` in Python means the *last* element of the list, which confuses callers with index `len(nums) - 1`.
`return -1` runs after the first miss because it's indented inside the `while` loop.
When `lo == hi` holds the target on the last step, the loop exits and wrongly returns `-1`.
Returning `-1` instead of `None` breaks `if binary_search(...)` truthiness checks.
fix: Return `None` instead of `-1` so callers don't index `nums[-1]` by mistake.
Check `if lo < len(nums) and nums[lo] == target: return lo` before returning `-1`.
Return `False` when `target` is not found.
Raise `ValueError` instead of returning `-1`.

explanation: The inclusive `[lo, hi]` range holds on every loop: an empty list exits immediately, a one-item list checks index 0, and every branch shrinks the interval.
